Quinault

Quinault Indian Nation’s Taholah planning account and Gary S. Morishima’s 2017 essay provide different routes into community decisions and stewardship. One describes a village-relocation planning phase; the other is an attributed argument for reciprocal relationships with public-land agencies. Neither is a current construction report or universal statement for all constituent communities.

Frank Tlyasman in a new dugout canoe at Taholah,1936
Unknown photographer; National Archives, NAID 519173(75-N-TAH-26). Public domain U.S. federal work / PDM 1.0.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — U.S. federal work; Public Domain Mark 1.0

The archive’s historical caption identifies Frank Tlyasman, using the period spelling Quinaielt, with his new dugout canoe at Taholah in 1936. This is one named person and moment, not all Quinault people, present membership, a government portrait or a claim about the canoe’s maker. The photographer is not identified; the record-creating agency is not falsely named as an individual photographer. Actual pixels show one person holding a paddle in a canoe, shoreline and trees; the full white archival print border remains visible. Complete available retrieved JPEG imported unchanged. Identity and context

The Quinault Indian Nation has homelands on the Pacific coast of Washington and includes distinct community histories.

Read the sources [1] quinaultindiannation.com

03

Taholah planning and community choices

The Nation explains that flooding and tsunami concerns motivated planning for Taholah’s lower village. Its project page records adoption of a master plan in June 2017 and describes community meetings, services and infrastructure choices. This reading concerns the planning rationale and participation; it does not claim that the page’s construction-stage statements remain current.

Read the sources [4] Quinault Indian Nation, Planning Department

04

Stewardship through reciprocal relationships

In his 2017 essay, Gary S. Morishima argues that stewardship of federal public lands needs substantive Native participation, mutual respect and reciprocity. He distinguishes engagement in decisions from merely gathering cultural information. Read this as a named author’s argument at a particular date, alongside Nation publications and later policy records.

Read the sources [2] Gary S. Morishima, Quinault Management Center; published by the National Park Service with permission

Open Eyes, Open Minds — Gary S. Morishima (2017) ↗

Morishima argues for substantive Native participation, reciprocity and respect in stewardship of federal public lands. Read it as his 2017 argument, distinct from both Nation legislation and a current NPS policy statement.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Author/date framing lines 19–29; selected opening argument 35–41 and stewardship/collaboration discussion 67–89, including the concluding recommendations. Other article sections and linked footnote works were not reviewed independently.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body read. The NPS says printed with the author’s permission; that is not permission to reuse his portrait. Historical policy references are treated as the author’s dated argument; underlying laws, reports, current agency policy and all footnotes were not checked. No disputed generalization about all Indigenous settlement patterns is adopted.

https://www.nps.gov/subjects/tek/gary-s-morishima-quinault-management-center-quinault-indian-nation.htm

Taholah Village Relocation — Project Background ↗

The Nation explains the relocation-planning rationale for Taholah, community involvement and the master plan adopted in June 2017. This project account should be read as a planning phase, with later construction status checked separately.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete substantive Project Background, The Plan, Process and Outcome prose, web lines 20–55. Staff contact details, population figures, maps and linked master-plan/environmental-assessment files were not adopted or separately inspected.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML read. The undated page describes a historical planning phase and expressly records June 2017 master-plan adoption; no assertion that its construction statements remain current in 2026. No independent hazard assessment, engineering advice, geographic boundary or project-completion claim.
